title: Wisconsin’s municipalities feeling the pinch of high fuel costs - WPR
text: Every month, Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway can see some of what the United States’ war with Iran is costing her constituents.  The cost to fuel both the city’s diesel and gasoline vehicles has increased by $222,580 a month since last year — a spike she attributes in part to the fighting with Iran and subsequent shipping disruptions. That monthly increase doesn’t include the city’s bus system. “It is serious and the impact of this unnecessary war and inflation is really impacting our budget,” Rhodes-Conway told “ Wisconsin Today .” “If we don’t see some relief on this soon, we’re going to be spending millions more for fuel this year, and that money has to come from somewhere, right? So that’s a direct impact to our taxpayers, to the essential services that we provide.” WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. Fuel costs are pinching municipal budgets around the state, and some of them could be forced to dip into their reserves to cover the added cost and make agonizing decisions for next year’s budgets, which are now being drafted. The city of Kaukauna — a city of about 18,000 people near Appleton — has seen fuel costs roughly double from last year, said Mayor Tony Penterman. So far, Kaukauna is under budget for the year. But with fall leaf pickup and winter snow plowing yet to come, which typically rack up a lot of miles for its diesel trucks, he is worried that the city won’t stay in the black.  “If we have a couple ice storms or snowstorms, at that $6.01 a gallon, that could put us over budget real fast in 2026 leading into 2027, which will be even more stressful,” Penterman said. The extra cost for fuel is putting pressure on other government functions. It drives up inflation, making street reconstruction or amenities like park pavilions more expensive. The city is due to upgrade its cybersecurity and is looking at hiring for new positions. Officials will have to make some tough decisions. “It’s hard to manage a city our size when you try to keep the tax rate under control,” Penterman said. Stevens Point Mayor Mike Wiza said his city is also feeling the pinch and has been looking for ways to conserve fuel. One has been to reduce idling time of city vehicles. “I don’t know how much it saves, but it’s something,” Wiza said. “If the vehicle is off for 15 minutes, you’re saving money.”  Figures provided by the city of Madison illustrate just how much monthly fuel bills can add up, especially for larger cities. Last September, the city paid $3.20 for a gallon of diesel. This September, the cost had climbed to $6.25 — an increase of $3.05 per gallon. The city was paying $2.90 a gallon for regular gasoline last September; that price jumped to $4.62.  Madison uses 50,000 gallons of diesel a month on average for its large fleet vehicles, which include fire trucks, garbage trucks and other public works vehicles. The Madison Metro bus system uses another 67,000 gallons of diesel a month. Madison’s gasoline fleet consumes, on average, 34,000 gallons a month.  The city doesn’t have many options for reducing fuel consumption. Police and fire trucks have to respond to calls, garbage has to be picked up, the buses need to run. “There’s some basic services that you just have to keep doing, and they have to use the fuel that they use,” Rhodes-Conway said. The city has traditionally bought some fuel with a contract that locks in a price. “Now, we don’t want to lock in a contract right now at this price because there’s a chance that it goes down and then we lose,” she said.  But the higher fuel costs underscore for the mayor the wisdom of the city’s efforts to invest in electric and hybrid vehicles.  “It doesn’t save us on diesel, but it does save us on gasoline because for every EV that we drive for 5,000 miles, that’s over 400 gallons of fuel that we’re saving that we don’t have to pay for,” Rhodes-Conway said. “Just saving on the fuel cost alone means that it makes sense for us to invest in these types of vehicles, so that we don’t have to deal with this volatility in the price of fossil fuels.”

title: Madison's police monitor is unique in Wisconsin. But the office has been dogged by controversies - WPR
text: In 2020, Madison’s Common Council voted to create the city’s first-ever independent police monitor. That vote, which followed years of advocacy, came toward the end of a public meeting that spanned nearly nine hours . During hours of public comment, most residents spoke in favor. The Office of Madison’s Independent Police Monitor intended to provide a civilian-led check on the Madison Police Department, and the powers of the position are unique in Wisconsin. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. But since its inception, the office has weathered controversy after controversy. Those disputes have involved heated public meetings, human resources investigations and a restraining order. The office — and the controversies surrounding it — are receiving heightened attention after a fatal police shooting on July 22. A total of four Madison cops are on leave after one of those officers, Kiel Baitinger-Peterson , shot Corey Ruiz , a 38-year-old Black resident. It will be up to Dane County’s district attorney to decide whether to charge the officers involved in that shooting, following a criminal investigation from Wisconsin’s Department of Justice. At the same time, the city’s interim police monitor, Aeiramique Glass, has launched her own investigation into the shooting . In protests that arose after the city moved to clear an encampment at the site of the shooting , Glass was involved in a physical altercation with police. In a video posted online, she said she would “f—ing burn this city to the ground.” The comments drew condemnation from the city’s mayor. But Glass doesn’t work for the mayor, and the mayor has no power to discipline or remove her. After the murder of George Floyd by a Minneapolis police officer in 2020, the number of communities adopting civilian oversight of police went up “fairly exponentially,” said Cameron McEllhiney, the executive director of the National Association for Civilian Oversight of Law Enforcement, or NACOLE. She says those efforts help bolster trust and improve transparency. “In the United States, we have a very polarized relationship between community and police,” McEllhiney said. “It’s a way for police to better understand the communities that they are serving (and) it’s a way for community to better understand police practices.” Nationwide, roughly 250 communities have some type of a police oversight agency, according to NACOLE. Many of those entities operate in large or mid-sized cities, but they vary widely in their powers and structure. In Wisconsin, the city’s police monitor and the civilian-led board that oversees it, are one-of-a-kind. “No other Wisconsin municipality has enacted ordinances establishing an agency or body charged with civilian oversight of its police department,” Madison’s city attorney wrote in a legal memo this summer. Under the ordinance that Madison adopted in 2020, the police monitor has the power to investigate complaints made by members of the public against Madison officers and the Madison Police Department. The monitor’s office can release conclusions from those reports, and it can make recommendations. Ultimately, however, the Office of the Independent Police Monitor, or OIPM, lacks the authority to discipline cops. That authority lies with the Police and Fire Commission , a separate city board that predates the monitor. Across the country, there are other cities where police monitors can review complaints and monitor critical policing incidents. In many communities, that monitor reports to the city council, the mayor or another executive, like a city manager. Madison’s situation, where the monitor is under the authority of a civilian oversight board, is less common but not unprecedented, McEllhiney said. When Madison adopted its ordinance, supporters argued that structure would help insulate the monitor from political pressure. They also wanted to make sure there was a seat at the table for community members, including those who might typically be left out of city politics. “When you have a person who’s been appointed by the mayor, there’s always the risk that the mayor will appoint someone who will only make decisions that they like,” said Sharon Fairley , a University of Chicago law professor, who previously worked as the chief administrator of Chicago’s Independent Police Review Authority. “Each structure has its pros and cons.” Madison’s structure has meant that — even as the mayor and some city council member express frustrations with the current police monitor — those elected officials have limited control over the situation. Madison’s ordinance says that the monitor reports directly to the executive subcommittee of the Police Civilian Oversight Board, or PCOB. The PCOB is responsible for nominating police monitors with the Common Council’s approval. PCOB Chair Maia Pearson did not respond to emailed questions from WPR. But based on public meetings and past statements, PCOB leadership appears to be standing behind the city’s current police monitor. More than a decade ago, Madison was reeling from another police shooting, after city officer Matt Kenny killed 19-year-old Tony Robinson in March 2015. That led to the creation of an ad hoc committee. That committee’s very first recommendation was to create an independent police monitor. The city’s Police Civilian Oversight Board met for the first time in November 2020. In late 2022, the PCOB hired attorney Robin Copley as the city’s first independent police monitor. That decision came after at least two other previously picked candidates backed out of consideration . After Copley started work, it took nearly two years for the monitor’s office to set up a form, so it could begin taking complaints. The office didn’t release its first annual report until 2025, and some council members raised concerns about Copley’s management and lack of response to public records requests . In October 2025, Copley resigned, citing medical reasons. Shortly before, the PCOB had convened a closed-session meeting to discuss her job performance. In fall 2025, the PCOB chose Aeiramique Glass as Madison’s interim police monitor. That job description said she was expected to serve for six to nine months, and that she would act as a hiring manager in the search for a permanent police monitor. In June, the Common Council voted unanimously to extend Glass’ contract through March 2027 , or until a permanent police monitor is hired. If that contract were to be terminated early, that decision would likely have to come from a Common Council vote, City Attorney Mike Haas told WPR. Glass previously served as Baltimore’s acting chief of police accountability. She filed a whistleblower lawsuit against Baltimore in 2025, alleging that she was terminated from that role in a discriminatory and retaliatory manner . Glass’ current annual salary is $147,741. When she took office in Madison, Glass said she encountered a backlog of 18 complaints against police, and she says she’s been steadily working through those. By spring 2026, eight complaints had been closed, according to an annual OIPM report which is dated to March 26 . The office has a staff of three people — Glass, a full-time office manager and part-time analyst Greg Gelembiuk. For 2026, the OIPM’s total operating budget was approved at $405,000. “The office is finally doing what it was created to do, and doing it without the resources necessary, without the staffing necessary,” Glass said in an interview with WPR this week. This spring, Glass released and then retracted her first annual report as monitor. The report included a cover image generated by artificial intelligence that hallucinated Madison’s skyline with two state Capitol buildings . Police Chief John Patterson also said that a section of the report included incorrect information about citations against juveniles. Glass said she used AI on a limited basis to create elements of the report and its cover image. She apologized, and later issued a revised version. “I really, truly take accountability for the ignorance of not really and truly understanding how much the skyline means to this community,” Glass said during a news conference. Despite missteps, Glass and her supporters also point to successes. Some of the office’s conclusions have been major. Earlier this year, the office released a report that disputed the official cause of death for 32-year-old Richard Lee Johnson. Dane County’s medical examiner previously concluded that Johnson died “accidentally due to complications from cocaine toxicity.” The OIPM, however, hired its own forensic pathologist, Dr. Victor Weedn, who concluded that, while cocaine may have contributed to Johnson’s death, the actual cause was cardiac arrest because of the way Johnson was restrained by police. After completing the OIPM report, Weedn was later hired by Dane County as a deputy medical examiner. As a result of that report, the OIPM and other city leaders urged the Dane County medical examiner’s office to reopen its investigation into Johnson’s cause and manner of death. It’s not clear whether the medical examiner has done so — the office’s director of operations Cristina Figueroa Soto did not respond to an inquiry from WPR. Meanwhile, top city officials including the city attorney, finance director and human resources director have been raising alarms about the monitor’s conduct. In an Aug. 31 memo to the Common Council president, those officials wrote that the OIPM was flouting multiple city procedures, including failing to meet budget deadlines and failing to follow rules for contracting and purchasing. The memo also alleged an OIPM staffer had been working remotely from another country without a valid telework agreement in place. In response, Glass has asserted that the OIPM does not have to follow city Administrative Procedure Memoranda, or APMs. “As you know, we do not have to comply with APMs other than what we do in good faith when I feel comfortable doing so,” Glass wrote to the city attorney on July 31. “I have never given you independent contractors’ information, and I will not start with this case.” According to the memo, the city has hired an external firm to investigate multiple human resources complaints involving OIPM staff. Meanwhile, Glass is embroiled in a dispute over access to MPD records from the shooting of Ruiz. Glass says Madison’s ordinance grants her unfettered access to those records. The city attorney argues that state law prevents police from releasing them while an investigation by the district attorney is still ongoing. That prompted Glass to file a lawsuit on Aug. 20, asking a judge to order the records’ release. Earlier in August, police released drone footage showing the altercation between Glass and police near where people were protesting. OIPM’s data analyst posted, then a deleted a video to Facebook, in which Glass talks to the camera just after the scuffle happened. In the video , Glass holds up her hand, which is bleeding. “They’ve been wanting to do this to me,” Glass says in the video. “I will f—ing burn this city down.” Glass has said she was speaking figuratively. “’I will burn this city down’ has been used throughout history as a metaphor for dismantling corruption, exposing injustice and demanding accountability,” the OIPM’s attorney William Sulton said at the time. PCOB leaders also defended Glass, saying the focus should be on the conduct of police. But Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway took a sharper tone. “I think it’s disturbing anytime a city employee is calling for violence,” Rhodes-Conway said at a news conference. In September, a Dane County judge granted a four-year restraining order to a Madison police officer who was involved with that incident. It orders Glass to stay away from that officer. In court documents, the officer wrote that Glass had grabbed her arm and pushed her. Some council members including Carmella Glenn and Julia Matthews have been staunch defenders of Monitor Glass. “Everybody hated her because she challenged the system,” Glenn said of some officials’ attitudes toward Glass. Other alders have emphasized that the role of the police monitor is vital, but say the office is failing to live up to its promise. “The operational conflicts and some of the divisiveness that has come from the office has gotten in the way of actually just doing that work,” Council President Sabrina Madison said. As an example, Madison pointed to a lengthy Facebook Live session , in which Glenn and Glass criticized multiple city employees by name. “I don’t want a monitor who’s going to sit on Facebook for two hours and drag a department agency and other alders, other community members,” Madison said. “I just don’t want that because that gets away from what the ordinance talks about (which is) building relationships.” Madison says she plans to use money from the Common Council’s budget to hire a mediator, so that she can meet with PCOB Chair Pearson and work through conflicts. This month, alders voted down a request to increase the OIPM’s budget by $28,500. And, during that discussion, many alders voiced concerns about OIPM operations. Among them was Alder Joann Pritchett, who alluded to Glass’ run-in with police in early August. “The monitor became the story when she inserted herself at the encampment site — that’s a no-no,” Pritchett said. “I have looked at my dictionary meaning of monitor, and it does not mean inserting yourself. It means standing back, making observations, making contemporaneous notes so that you know what happenened.” Glass told WPR she attends protests, so she can monitor what’s going on as part of her duties. Additionally, Madison’s OIPM ordinance specifies that the monitor should conduct “community outreach.” “I’m not really sure what they would perceive as participation in protest,” Glass said of her critics. “When I’m asked to be in community, that is a part of my job.” Fairley, a law professor who has studied civilian oversight, says it’s crucial that an independent monitor not be seen as overly for or against the local police. “Civilian oversight is supposed to be neutral,” Fairley said. “If you have a monitor that’s going out and protesting against the police, then the rank-and-file police officers are not going to think that they’re going to get a fair shot.” In an interview with WPR, Alder Will Ochowicz said he’s not necessarily opposed to the monitor attending protests. Rather, he says he concerns center around Glass’ management and job performance. “I want independent police oversight,” Ochowicz said at a September Common Council meeting. “But every single step of this has been adversarial between I.M. Glass and the city.” Just before his term expired this spring, former Alder MGR Govindarajan introduced an amendment , intended to beef up the OIPM’s reporting requirements and to clarify that the police monitor must follow city administrative procedures. Alders Yannette Figueroa Cole, Derek Field, Ochowicz and Madison signed on to that proposal. But, in the immediate aftermath of Ruiz’s death, all the sponsors agreed to withdraw their amendments. “At a moment when our community is grieving and looking to its leaders to strengthen trust in our systems of accountability, I believe it is important that we create space for collaboration rather than continue a process that many believe has become increasingly divisive,” Madison wrote in a blog post this July. The legislation could be reintroduced, although Madison and Ochowicz say they have no immediate plans to do so. There’s also the question of what the OIPM’s next budget will look like. Citing a shortfall, Rhodes-Conway instructed all department heads to submit proposals that cut their spending by at least 2 percent. The OIPM’s budget request, however, asks for that office’s operating budget to be increased to $781,158 in 2027. Additionally, Glass asked for $1.63 million in “emergency funding” for the OIPM, pointing to allocated OIPM funding that reverted to the city’s general fund after going unspent from 2000 to 2025. Going forward, Glass has also urged city officials to set a funding floor for the OIPM at 1 percent of the MPD budget. The department’s 2026 operating budget is more than $98 million . Glass did not submit a budget narrative form or formal transmittal memo by the city’s deadline for department heads of July 17. Instead, she sent a letter on July 27, explaining why she did not follow that process. “This letter is formal notice that the Office of the Independent Police Monitor needs immediate action, not the routine budget process,” Glass wrote . “I was in the process of preparing the narrative and explanation forms that accompany that submission when this community experienced the killing of a Black man by police, and my attention turned to this office’s rapid response and to the community in the aftermath. What I submitted in Munis was an attempt to participate in a budget process that is not, in its current form, an equitable one.” Ruiz was shot on July 22, five days after the deadline for agency budget requests. Rhodes-Conway will submit her operating budget proposal next week. And ultimately, the Common Council will vote on how much money the police monitor’s office should get. title: Signal chat for alders is legal, but still raises questions - Madison365
text: A group chat among Madison alders using the secure messaging app Signal is legal, as long as no Common Council business is discussed, City Attorney Mike Haas said. But a freedom of information advocate said it still raises questions because the app’s disappearing messages function makes it impossible to know whether Alders used it to discuss proposals before the council. One Signal group chat brought to Madison365’s attention has been active since April 2025, started by former alder MGR Govindaranjan following that spring election. It currently has eight members, but has previously had as many as 12. Various members have set the “disappearing messages” function to automatically delete messages at varying intervals from eight hours to one week, according to screen shots obtained by Madison365. Why Signal raises questions Signal is regarded as one of the most secure messaging apps, as it employs end-to-end encryption and does not store messages or user data on a central server. That means once messages are received and deleted, they’re gone forever and can’t be retrieved or released, even under a court order. That raises an open records question for Bill Lueders, president of the Wisconsin Freedom of Information Council. “My question is, why are they using Signal Chat?” Lueders said. “It seems to me the only distinction or advantage is that it allows them to communicate secretly without people being able to have a record of their communication, which to me sounds like they’re trying to break the law.” The use of any messaging app – even email – also raises questions regarding open meetings law, which prohibits discussion of official business among a quorum of members (in Madison, that means 14) without public notice. In fact, the City of Madison posts public notices of social functions where 14 or more Alders might be in attendance. In his onboarding presentation for new alders , Haas notes that it’s also prohibited to gather enough members to potentially form a negative quorum – that is, enough potential votes to block any proposal. In some cases, that could be as few as five; 12 would always constitute a negative quorum. In 2020, then-City Attorney Michael May wrote in a formal opinion that any meeting of five or more alders should be given public notice. But neither open records law nor the open meetings law, nor the relevant city of Madison ordinances, would be applicable to purely personal conversations.  Every Alder who responded to questions from Madison365 said the Signal group chat in question was only used for personal communications. Some said Signal was used in other instances for communication regarding City business, but that they saved such messages to comply with open records law. Council Friends 2025 Screen shots provided to Madison365 indicate that Govindaranjan started the group, called “Council Friends 2025,” on April 15, 2025, two weeks after the April 1 spring election and the day the new council was sworn in. Messages were initially set to disappear after eight hours; District 1 Alder John Duncan, who has since left the council and the chat group, disabled disappearing messages. “Good idea to have disappearing messages off, I think,” Govindarajan wrote in the group. “Main reminder for this group: no city business can be discussed here.” He then announced that the group would have a “friends hangout/election-celebration” at the Paradise bar in Madison the following Saturday. According to the screenshots, then-newly-elected alder Carmella Glenn, who is now vice president of the Council, reactivated the disappearing messages function and set it to delete messages after eight hours on April 21.  Glenn told Madison365 that she didn’t recall activating that setting. “I apologize. I was not thinking about open records,” she said. “I didn’t even know enough about open records. It was my first day.” No screenshots reviewed by Madison365 indicate that anyone disabled the disappearing messages function in the nearly 18 months since. In fact, several members adjusted the timing of automatic message deletion. Screen shots indicate that Govindarajan left the group after the spring 2026 election, in which he did not run for re-election, and Duncan left the group in July, when he resigned his seat because he was moving out of the city. Govindaranjan made District 10 Alder Yanette Figueroa Cole the group’s administrator. Both she and Council President Sabrina Madison left the group on July 24, two days after Madison police shot and killed Corey Ruiz. Neither answered a question from Madison365 asking why they left the group. Figueroa Cole made Alder Julia Matthews administrator of the group when she left. As of September 28, eight members remained in the group: Glenn, Matthews, and Alders Derek Fields, Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford, John Guequirre, Regina Vidaver, Sean O’Brien and Will Ochowicz.  Madison365 sent a number of questions to all the current members of the group; those who responded said they only used the group for personal purposes such as scheduling social gatherings and sharing news or announcements.  “I use Signal as an easy way to share news and for social planning in a more secure platform than texting,” Vidaver wrote in an email to Madison365. “I do not remember any Council business being conducted in the Signal group.” “The chat referenced (in Madison365’s questions) was not used for the purpose of conducting official communications and therefore does not fall within the retention requirement outlined in” Madison ordinances, Figueroa Cole wrote. “The chat was created originally as a post-election for current and newly elected alders who had met before the election,” Ochowicz wrote. “No city business was discussed in the chat, it was mainly to notify of events like parties or barbeques, or to share notifications from Voces De Fronteras on ICE sightings.” “Shortly after I joined the Council in January 2024, one or more alders shared that the Signal app had been used for some time for non-city business, that is, social interactions,” Guequirre wrote. “I had not used the app previously, but saw no objection to the platform for the described purpose … Typical chats have involved (1) where to meet socially, (2) event recommendations, (3) reading recommendations, (4) other social interactions. Two of the longest chats I can remember involved vacation photos and recipes … I hesitate to say Council and Committee business has never been discussed because it takes a little time to absorb all of the nuances of the open meetings and open records laws. When business ends up in a post, veteran alders are quick to ‘coach’ the novices.” No alders who responded to Madison365 acknowledged being members of other Signal groups; screenshots from a different group administered by Martinez-Rutherford indicate she shut it down after receiving questions from Madison365. That group had 11 members, four of whom are no longer members of the council, and a former alder who was a member said the group was not active and she wasn’t even aware the group existed until she got a notification that the group had been closed. Guequirre and Glenn both gave examples of council business being discussed via Signal outside the group chat.  Guequirre said he received a Signal message from Vidaver about cosponsorship of a resolution; knowing that constituted City business, he saved the message, he said. Glenn provided screen shots to Madison365 showing messages from Figueroa Cole containing background information on funding for a men’s homeless shelter. Figueroa Cole had the messages set to delete after one day; Glenn took a screen shot for records retention purposes. Glenn said after receiving an open records request in August, she started to realize the potential problems of using Signal, especially among so many members. “I want it to stop,” she said. What the law says Madison General Ordinance says city officials, which includes city employees as well as elected alders, “shall refrain” from communicating via text message or instant messaging “for official communications purposes or for matters that would result in a public record if another format such as email or written communications were employed, unless the employee or official preserves a copy of such communications.” Haas said that means personal communications via text or instant message are allowed, as personal communications do not constitute public records, and that it’s also permissible to discuss official business if those messages are saved. The same is true on the open meetings question: it’s permissible for more than five alders to gather or have a conversation, as long as they don’t discuss city business. But due to the nature of Signal, the media and the community are left to take officials at their word that they’re not using it to discuss city business. Other forms of communication are generally preserved, and even if alders exclude communications they deem as personal from open records requests, a court could adjudicate otherwise and compel such records be released. “Rightly or wrongly, the state’s open meetings law seeks to ensure that the deliberative process plays out in public, that people aren’t going around cutting backdoor deals and reaching decisions outside of the public forum where they meet as a body,” said Lueders of the Freedom of Information Council. “They’re supposed to hash out their government business in a public setting. Those deliberations are supposed to be taking place in a public venue and not behind closed doors and not behind closed apps.”

title: Air Force veteran Gregory McClain to lead Madison Department of Civil Rights - Madison365
text: Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway has appointed Gregory McClain as the next director of the Madison Department of Civil Rights. McClain will begin the new position on Monday, Oct. 12. McClain is an Air Force veteran who most recently served as the Equal Opportunity Manager for Montgomery County Government in Rockville, Maryland. He has more than a decade of experience working in racial equity, social justice, equal employment and public health. “Greg will be a fantastic addition to the Department of Civil Rights. His journey to civil rights work makes him well-qualified to lead this agency with a data-driven approach focused on results for our residents,” Rhodes-Conway said in a statement. McClain holds a bachelor’s degree in biomedical sciences and master’s degrees in business and health administration from Oklahoma State University. He also earned a master’s degree in public health from UW–Madison, where he worked in the community on efforts to prevent harm among veterans and others experiencing substance use disorders and to advance health equity. “I’m grateful for the opportunity to serve Madison residents and grow the impact of the Department of Civil Rights,” McClain said. “Starting from a place of honesty and transparency, I see my role as ensuring it’s a great city for everyone.” McClain said he plans to support the department’s existing work while expanding its impact. “I fully intend to be a champion of the department and can’t wait to amplify the important work being done by its dedicated staff,” he said.

A Community Resilience Hub builds on a trusted, local community space that is familiar to residents, and expands its capabilities to support the neighborhood during emergencies.   Madison can experience events like severe weather, extreme temperatures, power outages, poor air quality, and floods. Community Resilience Hubs can provide information and resources to help residents respond to and recover from those events close to home. title: New resilience hubs aim to help Madison residents during weather emergencies - WMTV 15 NEWS
text: MADISON, Wis. (WMTV) - The City of Madison is providing people with safe, reliable locations during an emergency. Officials are creating a network of Community Resilience Hubs. The hubs will be available for people to go to during emergencies such as severe weather, extreme temperatures, power outages, poor air quality or flooding. The city says the spaces will be able to provide resources and information to help people recover from those emergencies. This could include distribution of supplies, a place to charge a device, relief from the elements or disaster recovery resources. “As our climate changes, Madison is experiencing more dangerous weather events that disrupt our daily lives,” said Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway. “Community Resilience Hubs offer an efficient way to connect the community with needed resources, closer to where people live, and provide support until conditions return to normal.” Currently, Madison has two locations within the network. Boys and Girls Clubs of Dane County’s Allied Family Center and Wisconsin Youth Company’s Elver Park Neighborhood Center will act as hubs. The city hopes to expand the network and work with other community organizations looking to support their neighbors. title: Madison officials say city is ready to manage clerk’s maternity leave during election - Wisconsin Examiner
text: Madison officials say the city is prepared to manage Clerk Lydia McComas' maternity leave during the Nov. 3 election, even with the added scrutiny that comes with recent high-profile errors. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner) Madison City Clerk Lydia McComas took over her job in September 2025 with the city under heavy scrutiny from state election officials after nearly 200 absentee ballots were lost during the 2024 election. During the April 2026 state Supreme Court election, 23 late arriving absentee ballots nearly weren’t counted after a staff error. Ann Jacobs, a Democrat on the Wisconsin Elections Commission, said at a meeting in April that the second error was “absurd.” The two problems made the city of Madison the subject of the first two investigations ever opened by WEC. In June, Votebeat reported that McComas told Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway that she would “firmly address the lack of communication” that caused the mistake and the clerk’s office would have more staff in place for the August and November elections. But McComas will be on maternity leave during the Nov. 3 election. Despite McComas’ absence, city officials say the processes put in place to avoid repeated errors, additional staff and help from other city departments will be enough to smoothly manage the midterm elections and the potential scrutiny that could come from WEC or the Republican Party of Wisconsin — whose gubernatorial candidate this year, Tom Tiffany, has previously cast doubt on election results from Wisconsin’s largest cities. City spokesperson Dylan Brogan said of the recent errors in Madison that the city is “confident these things won’t happen again.” “This is a team process that involves 2,000 people,” he said. In McComas’ absence, deputy clerk Kaitlyn Bernarde is running the election. Brogan said that other city staff, such as City Attorney Mike Haas, who previously served as the WEC administrator, can help fill in. Bernarde spent more than four years as the clerk in Wausau, a credential that convinced WEC the transition wouldn’t be a problem. “[McComas] hired a new deputy who was the clerk out of Wausau. Based on that we didn’t have any concerns,” Jacobs told the Wisconsin Examiner. In an interview with the Examiner, Bernarde said prior to the August primary elections, the clerk’s office added a staff member who is responsible for managing the thousands of absentee ballots returned to the city, which she believes will prevent any further absentee-related errors. “That is one of our major new changes in our office, we implemented an absentee lead position before the August election, and so we have a full time staff member who’s in charge of that, as well as additional hourly staff and other city staff who are helping to ensure that we have checks in place in the system, that we can check in at different points to make sure that we’re on track to get ballots out on time to our AM delivery, our PM delivery, as well as any late deliveries throughout the day so that way some of those similar mistakes don’t happen again.” Bernarde also said that the city and election staff are prepared to run the midterms under scrutiny from WEC and outside observers. “I think Madison always kind of is under scrutiny by the state, our residents and other people who are involved in the process, and so we’ve had experience working under that kind of pressure the last couple elections,” she said. “And we all want a zero [error] election, and so we talk through that with our staff, with our poll workers to ensure that we are trained and that we document any instances that happen. Because elections involve humans and so sometimes mistakes happen but we have processes in place to confront them, minimize them and then also respond to address them appropriately after.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. by Henry Redman, Wisconsin Examiner October 6, 2026 by Henry Redman, Wisconsin Examiner October 6, 2026 Madison City Clerk Lydia McComas took over her job in September 2025 with the city under heavy scrutiny from state election officials after nearly 200 absentee ballots were lost during the 2024 election. title: Mayor’s budget staves off deeper cuts with one-time $7.5 million influx to Metro - Wisconsin State Journal
text: Madison could put off major spending cuts for another year under Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway's proposed $477.5 million operating budget for 2027, which largely spares the police, fire and other departments. Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said the city will continue to fully fund newly introduced operating expenses, including its 10th ambulance unit, the Imagination Center Library and Bratillon Drive men’s homeless shelter. The average Madison homeowner would see a roughly $84 increase in the city property tax bill, a $20.67 increase from Dane County, and a $311.82 increase from the Madison Metropolitan School District, for a total of about $416.50.
